content: The 2017 World Rapid Chess Championship was won by Indian grandmaster Vishwanathan Anand on 28 December 2017 [5]. Prior to this, the title was jointly recognized by FIDE [5]. Previous winners of the World Rapid Chess Championship include Vassily Ivanchuk of Ukraine in 2016 [1], Levon Aronian, who won the Chess World Cup 2017 [3], and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, who won the World Rapid Chess Championship in 2013 and 2016 [4].

The United States abandoned the gold standard in March and April 1933 [3]. The Federal Reserve was forced to raise interest rates to protect the gold standard for the US dollar, but this worsened economic pressures [1]. In 1971, the U.S. government suspended the convertibility of the U.S. dollar to gold [2].

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was built in 2008 [2]. The vault officially opened on February 26, 2008, although the first seeds arrived in January 2008 [2]. The Norwegian government funded the vault's construction, which was scheduled to open in late 2008 [3].

The national anthem of Trinidad and Tobago is titled Forged from the Love of Liberty. It was composed by Patrick S. Castagne [1][3]. The anthem was originally composed as the national anthem for the West Indies Federation, which lasted from 1958-1962, and was later adopted by Trinidad and Tobago after it achieved independence in 1962 [1]. Patrick Castagne was a renowned West Indian songwriter who was employed at the Trinidad and Tobago Commission in London at the time [1].

Bourbon Street is a famous street in New Orleans' French Quarter, known for its many bars and strip clubs [1]. St. Charles Avenue is another notable thoroughfare, featuring mansions and the St. Charles Streetcar Line [2]. Royal Street is known for its antique shops, art galleries, and hotels [3][5]. Frenchmen Street is known for its live-music venues, restaurants, and businesses [4].

The Beatles' song "Do You Want to Know a Secret?" was sung by George Harrison in their 1963 album "Please Please Me" [1]. The song was primarily composed by John Lennon but was credited to Lennon-McCartney [1]. Though Lennon initially wrote the song with himself in mind, he realized it was better suited for Harrison [2]. A cover of the song by Billy J. Kramer and the Dakotas was also released [1].

Based on provided documents, the 13th Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified by the states on December 6, 1865 [1][2]. This amendment was passed by the Senate on April 8, 1864, and by the House on January 31, 1865 [2]. The ratifications from North Carolina and Georgia provided the final votes needed for it to become part of the Constitution [1]. The Thirteenth Amendment became part of the Constitution on December 6, 1865, as certified by Secretary of State Seward on December 18, 1865 [1].

"Don't Matter to Me" is a song by Canadian musician Drake featuring posthumous vocals from American singer and songwriter Michael Jackson, from Drake's fifth studio album "Scorpion" (2018) [1][2]. It was sent to British contemporary hit radio on July 6, 2018 as the album's fourth single [1][2]. Commercially, the song has [1].

England won the World Cup in soccer in 1966 during the tournament held in their home country [1][2][4]. They defeated West Germany 4–2 in the final, winning the Jules Rimet Trophy [1]. This was England's only FIFA World Cup title [1]. The final was played on 30th July 1966 [1]. Notable performances in the tournament were made by debutants Portugal, who ended third, and North Korea, who made it to the quarter finals [1].

Booker T. Washington addressed both African Americans and white Americans in his Atlanta Exposition Speech [1][3]. In the speech, Washington urged blacks to focus on work and education rather than demanding political rights [2]. This speech laid the foundation for the Atlanta Compromise, which established an understanding between African-American leaders and Southern white leaders [3]. The Atlanta Exposition Speech was delivered before a predominantly white audience at the Cotton States and International Exposition in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1895 [3]. The Atlanta Exposition was held in Piedmont Park, with attractions including Buffalo Bill's Wild West Show, the Liberty Bell, and the first public demonstration of C. Francis Jenkins and Thomas Armat's motion picture projection device [5].

In the 1952 session, Alabama passed a right-to-work law at the urging of then Governor Robert F. Kennon [5]. However, the law was repealed in 1956 [5]. The right-to-work law was reinstituted in Alabama in 1976 [2].

The first North American Indigenous Games were held in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada in 1990 [1]. The dream to hold a multi-sport event for indigenous North American athletes began in the 1970s, with events such as the Native Summer Games in Enoch, Alberta, Canada in 1971 [2]. The Games are governed by the North American Indigenous Games Council, consisting of representatives from 13 provinces and territories in Canada and 13 regions in the United States [2]. The most recent games took place in Toronto, Ontario, Canada in 2017 [3].

Stephen King's Dark Tower series consists of eight books [1][2]. These books, which include "The Gunslinger," "Wizard and Glass," and "The Dark Tower," make up a combined total of approximately 4,250 pages [1]. Additionally, other books by Stephen King, such as "It," "The Stand," and "Salem's Lot," are linked to this series or referred to within it [2]. The series has expanded upon King's multiverse, connecting many of his other novels [1]. According to King, the series can be seen as one long über-novel [3]. A ninth book titled "The Wind Through the Keyhole" was also announced, but the specific number of books in the series as a whole is not explicitly stated [3].

The Ferris wheel known as the Myrtle Beach SkyWheel is located in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina [1]. This wheel is the second-tallest extant Ferris wheel in North America and was the tallest in the United States east of the Mississippi River when it opened in May 2011 [1]. The wheel is designed by Ronald Bussink Professional Rides and manufactured by Chance Morgan [1]. The Myrtle Beach SkyWheel has 42 glass-enclosed, temperature-controlled gondolas [1]. The Ferris wheel operates year-round and has a height of 187 feet [2].

In the United States, the third season of Rick and Morty aired on Cartoon Network's late-night programming block, Adult Swim [1][2]. It premiered on April 1, 2017, with "The Rickshank Rickdemption" [1]. The remaining episodes began airing weekly on July 30, 2017 [1].

In this context, linking a currency value to the value of gold is referred to as the gold standard [1][2][3]. This system declares that a country's government will exchange its currency for a certain weight in gold [2]. The gold standard works on the assumption that there are no restrictions on capital movements or export of gold by private citizens across countries [2]. The value of the dollar being linked to gold for a significant portion of American history is mentioned in [3]. In a gold standard, a currency's value is linked to that of gold instead of a foreign currency, which is a special case of a currency board [4].

Football was first introduced in the Olympics at the 1928 Summer Olympics [3]. At this time, it was the last Olympic football tournament before the first FIFA World Cup in 1930. Prior to 1928, the Olympic football tournament had represented the World Championship of football [3]. The tournament at the 1984 Summer Olympics was the first to allow professionals [1][2].

The Cleveland Browns returned to the NFL in 1999, after a three-year period of deactivation [1]. Their return was facilitated by Lerner, who purchased the franchise after bidding for the right to buy it [2]. The 1999 season marked the first time professional football was played in Cleveland since the 1995 season [3].

St. Petersburg is a city in Pinellas County, Florida [1][2]. It is the second-largest city in the Tampa Bay Area, after Tampa, and is part of the Tampa–St. Petersburg–Clearwater Metropolitan Statistical Area [1]. The county seat is Clearwater, but St. Petersburg is the largest city in Pinellas County [3]. The city is located on the Pinellas peninsula between Tampa [1].

In 1888, George Eastman introduced the first handheld amateur camera, the Kodak camera [3]. Thomas Edison developed a portable film camera in 1896 [1]. Polish inventor Kazimierz Prószyński first demonstrated a hand-held film camera in 1898, but it was not reliable [1]. In 1908 with a hand-held Lumière camera, Wilbur Wright was filmed flying his aircraft on the outskirts of Paris [1]. Handheld electronic cameras, in the sense of a device meant to be carried and used like a handheld film camera, appeared in 1981 with the demonstration of the Sony Mavica (Magnetic Video Camera) [2].

The White Queen in the film "Alice Through the Looking Glass" is played by Anne Hathaway [1]. In this film, the White Queen's name is Mirana of Marmoreal [1]. Hathaway portrayed the White Queen as a "punk-rock vegan pacifist" [2]. The White Queen is shown to have a habit of holding her hands gracefully at shoulder height in most scenes she appears in [1]. The White Queen is played by Phyllis Diller in the 1987 version of the film [4].

In 1860, Christopher Memminger was asked to write the "Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union", outlining the reasons for secession [1]. William Henry Gist was one of the signers of the Ordinance of Secession on December 20, 1860 [2]. During the secession convention in South Carolina, Francis Wilkinson Pickens proposed a motion to repeal the Ordinance of Secession, though it was not passed [3]. The Ordinance of Secession is the general name given to documents drafted and ratified by each of the thirteen southern states and the Territory of Arizona formally seceding from the United States [4].

The Rio Olympics had a cost of $4.6 billion for direct capital costs related to the competition venues, Olympic village, international broadcast center, and media and press center [1]. The total bid expenses for the Applicant and Candidature phases were R$85,792 million for the Rio de Janeiro bid committee [3]. The Oxford Olympics Study 2016 estimated the out-turn cost of the Rio 2016 Summer Olympics at USD 4.6 billion in 2015-dollars, including sports-related costs such as operational costs, technology, transportation, workforce, and administration costs, among others [4]. Compared to other Games, the cost for Moscow 1980, Beijing 2008, and Sochi 2014 were significantly higher, with costs of $4.6 billion for Rio 2016, $40-44 billion for Beijing 2008, and $51 billion for Sochi 2014 [1][5]. The average cost for the Summer Games since 1960 is $5.2 billion [5].

The festival of Holi marks the end of winter and the beginning of spring [1][2]. It is also seen as a day to meet others, play and laugh, forget and forgive, and repair broken relationships [1]. The festival signifies the victory of good over evil [1]. Hindus believe that Holi festivities mark the beginning of the new year as well as an occasion to reset and renew ruptured relationships, end conflicts, and rid themselves of accumulated emotional impurities from the past [3]. The night before Holi, bonfires are lit in a ceremony known as Holika Dahan [3]. The next day, Holi, also known as "Dhuli" in Sanskrit, is celebrated [3]. Holi is celebrated at the end of winter, on the last full moon day of the Hindu luni-solar calendar month marking the spring [2]. The date varies with the lunar cycle and typically falls in March [2].

The song "Brown Eyes" is from Fleetwood Mac's 1979 double LP "Tusk" [1]. It was composed and sung by Christine McVie [1]. Original guitarist Peter Green also took part in the sessions for "Brown Eyes", but his playing on the track is not credited on the album [1].

In Big Brother 10, Dan was crowned the winner in a Jury vote of seven to zero [5].

The territory of present-day southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico that is known as the Gadsden Purchase was bought from Mexico via a treaty that took effect on June 8, 1854 [1]. The first draft of the treaty was signed on December 30, 1853, by James Gadsden, U.S. ambassador to Mexico, and by Antonio López de Santa Anna, president of Mexico [1]. The U.S. Senate voted in favor of ratifying the treaty with amendments on April 25, 1854, and it was then transmitted to President Franklin Pierce [1].

The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) was established by Reverend John Flynn on 15 May 1928 in Cloncurry, Queensland [1]. This date marks the start of the RFDS service, which was a response to the medical needs of isolated communities [1][2].

The song "Genie in a Bottle" was released on June 22, 1999 [1]. It was the lead single from Christina Aguilera's self-titled debut album [1]. The song became the biggest summer song of 1999 [2]. It reached number one on the "Billboard" Hot 100 and stayed there for five consecutive weeks [2]. The single received generally favorable reviews from contemporary music critics [1]. "Genie in a Bottle" received a significant amount of airplay and CD sales [2].

The second season of Jessica Jones started on Netflix on March 8, 2018 [1]. The second season was released to coincide with International Women's Day [1]. The season was produced in April 2017 and concluded in September 2017 [3].

In the transition from Roman Britain to post-Roman Britain, the end of Roman rule occurred at different times and under different circumstances [1]. In 383, the usurper Magnus Maximus likely left local warlords in charge [1]. Around 410, the Romano-Britons expelled the magistrates of the usurper Constantine III [1].It's important to note that this is highly complex and nuanced period of history, various interpretations characterize the events, some argue Rome chose to abandon Britain, while others argue it was the Britons leaving Rome [5].

During the 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, the Olympic torch was carried into the stadium by Sir Steve Redgrave [1][2]. He then passed the torch to a team of seven young athletes, each chosen to reflect the 'Inspire a Generation' theme of the 2012 Games [1]. James Beckham had previously brought the torch to the stadium via the Limehouse Cut on a speedboat [2].

The Latin term "camera obscura" means "dark room" [1][2]. It refers to a natural optical phenomenon where an image of a scene at the other side of a screen is projected through a small hole in the screen as a reversed and inverted image [1][3]. This phenomenon was used as an aid for drawing and painting [4].

The Boston Red Sox set a franchise record for wins in a season in 2018, finishing with 108 victories [2]. Prior to this, the most wins the Red Sox had in a season was in 1912, with a record of 105 wins and 47 losses [3]. This season also saw them set the record for highest winning percentage (.691) in a season, a record that still stands [3].
Britain's Got Talent series 9 was won by dog tricks duo Jules O'Dwyer & Matisse [1]. This series aired from 11 April to 31 May 2015 [3].

Cricket was introduced to India through the East India Company, which transformed from a commercial trading venture into one that ruled India as it acquired auxiliary governmental and military functions [1]. The East India Company, in effect, founded the city of Madras in 1639 and acquired Portuguese territory on the west coast of India in 1661, which included Bombay [1]. The earliest reference to cricket being played in India is dated 1721, when British sailors of the East India Company were reported to be playing cricket at Cambay, near Baroda [3]. The Oriental Cricket Club, established by the Parsi community in Mumbai in 1848, was the first cricket club in India [4].

However, in another source, The Phantom Stallion is identified as a silver stallion, half Quarter Horse and Half Mustang [1]. This shows that there might be different interpretations of the term "Black Stallion" in different contexts.

The most plentiful category of rock in Earth's crust is igneous rock, making up about 64.7% of the Earth's crust by volume [1]. Specifically, most major igneous rocks are found along a sequence known as Bowen's reaction series, with about 66% consisting of basalts and gabbros, 16% granite, and 17% granodiorites and diorites [1]. Oceanic crust, which underlies ocean basins, is composed of dense iron magnesium silicate igneous rocks, like basalt [2].

Elvin Bishop wrote "Fooled Around and Fell in Love" and it was performed by him, but the lead vocals are sung by Mickey Thomas [1]. The song was a hit in 1976, peaking at #3 on the "Billboard" Hot 100 singles chart [1]. Other artists such as Henry Lee Summer, Mark Wills, Rod Stewart, and The Winery Dogs have also covered the song [3]. Priscilla Bowman originally recorded the song in 1958 [5].
The song "As Time Goes By" was written by Herman Hupfeld in 1931 [1][3]. It gained widespread fame in 1942 when it was sung in the movie "Casablanca" [1].

The systolic blood pressure is the peak pressure in the arteries, which occurs near the end of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles are contracting [1]. An example of normal measured values for a resting, healthy adult human is 120 mmHg systolic and 80 mmHg diastolic (written as 120/80 mmHg) [1][5]. The pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer when the sound first starts again in the artery [4].

Abbe Raven, a theatre and film academic, was married to Martin Tackel, an attorney and commercial arbitrator [4]. There Will Be Blood, a 2007 drama film, is set during Southern California's oil boom of the late 19th and early 20th centuries [2]. The play "Brave Blood," by Robert O'Hara, on the other hand, takes place in the home of a psychiatrist who takes in a group of female prostitutes, with the investigation of a murder throwing the house into chaos [1].
The first televised Monday Night Football game, which took place in 1970, was between the Cleveland Browns and the New York Jets [1][4]. The Jets lost the game by a score of 31-21 [4].

The New England Patriots won the Super Bowl three times in four years, specifically in 2001, 2003, and 2004 [1]. However, they did not win the Super Bowl in a row. The last team to win back-to-back Super Bowls was the Seattle Seahawks, who defeated the Panthers in 2014 [2]. The Patriots' streak of multiple Super Bowl wins ended with their second playoff game loss the following year [2].

Network address translation (NAT) is a method of remapping one IP address space into another [1][2][3]. It is a popular and essential tool in conserving global IP address space in the face of IPv4 address exhaustion [1][2]. NAT modifies network address information in packets [1][3]. In this method, one Internet-routable IP address of a NAT gateway can be used for an entire private network [1]. The technique that hides an entire IP address space is usually referred to as IP masquerading, which is virtually synonymous with NAT [3].

The How to Train Your Dragon 3 movie, titled How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World, was originally set to be released in 2016 [1]. However, the release date was delayed several times and ultimately set for February 22, 2019 [2].

In the 2000 live-action film "How the Grinch Stole Christmas!", Cindy Lou Who is played by actress Taylor Momsen [1]. Additionally, American child actress and model Emily Grace Reaves may be recognized for her role as Cindy Lou in an unspecified title [3].

The ribeye steak comes from the rib section of beef, specifically spanning from ribs six through twelve [1]. It is primarily composed of the longissimus dorsi muscle but also includes the complexus and spinalis muscles [1]. In the United States, the ribeye steak or Spencer steak refers to a rib steak with the bone removed, while in Australia and New Zealand, "ribeye" is used when this cut is served with the bone in, and it is called "Scotch fillet" when the bone is removed [3]. The ribeye steak is flavorful and tender, deriving from the lightly worked upper rib cage area [3].

The Lion King debuted on Broadway on October 15, 1997, in previews, with the official opening on November 13, 1997, at the New Amsterdam Theater [1]. The Broadway production moved to the Minskoff Theatre in 2006 [1]. The West End production of The Lion King debuted in October 1999 [2].

The Golden State Warriors are based in Oakland, California [1][2]. They play their home games at the Oracle Arena [1]. The team was relocated to the San Francisco Bay Area in 1962 [4]. Prior to the 1971–72 season, the team changed its geographic moniker to Golden State [1].

The music for the film How to Train Your Dragon was composed by John Powell [1]. This is his sixth collaboration with DreamWorks Animation [4]. The score was released by Varèse Sarabande on March 23, 2010 [1]. The score also won the International Film Music Critics Association 2011 Awards for Best Original Score for an Animated Feature [1].

The first man-made object to enter space was the German A4 rocket, launched on October 3, 1942 [2]. Prior to this, the record for the highest-known projectile was held by the Paris Gun shells during World War One, which reached at least 40 kilometers altitude [5]. However, the first liquid-fueled rocket was launched by Robert Goddard on March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts [4]. The German scientist Hermann Noordung imagined a complete space station in his book "The Problem of Space Travel" in 1929 [1].
Hungry Jack's has more than 390 locations across Australia [1][4]. The company Hungry Jack's currently owns and operates, or sub-licenses all of the Hungry Jack's restaurants in Australia [2].

The song is performed when Joseph is at his lowest point, almost giving up on his faith and deciding to trust fully in God [2][3]. PluggedIn explains the song's meaning as "Persevering through dark times can yield great rewards. God’s role in Joseph’s comeback" [2]. The film received mixed to positive reviews, with critics praising the animation, storytelling, and music [1].

The song was written by BC Jean and Toby Gad, who also handled its production alongside Beyoncé [1]. Beyoncé recorded her own version after the song was originally recorded by BC Jean, whose record company rejected it [1][2]. Jean was initially upset when she learned that Beyoncé was releasing it as a single, but eventually, they reached an agreement [1][4].

The film is a modernization of William Shakespeare's late-16th century comedy "The Taming of the Shrew" set in a late-1990s American high school [2][3].

In association football (soccer), substitutions are allowed during stoppages in play, subject to the referee's permission [1][3]. A maximum of three substitutions are allowed during a match, with an additional substitution permitted if the game goes into extra-time [1][5]. The outgoing player must leave the field before the substitute enters [3]. The substitute can only enter the field at the halfway line [3]. In contrast, the United States national beach soccer team can make as many substitutions as they want while the play is still going on [2]. In ice hockey and basketball, substitutions are permitted during stoppages, but are otherwise unlimited [4].

Thomas Robert Malthus wrote An Essay on the Principle of Population, a book published anonymously in 1798 [1]. The author was later identified as Malthus [1]. The book predicted a grim future due to the exponential growth of the population compared to the arithmetic growth of food production [1]. Malthus' writing fuelled debate about the size of population [1]. He wrote a summary of his essay in 1830, titled A Summary View on the Principle of Population [3].

The region now known as Mumbai was called "Bombaim" in Portuguese during the Portuguese rule from 1534 to 1661 [1][2]. The name "Bombaim" possibly originated as the Galician-Portuguese phrase "bom baim", meaning "good little bay" [4]. In 1516, Portuguese explorer Duarte Barbosa used the name "Tana-Maiambu", where "Tana" refers to the adjoining town of Thane and "Maiambu" might refer to Mumbadevi [4]. Other variations recorded in the 16th and 17th centuries include "Mombayn", "Bombay", "Bombain", "Bombaym", "Monbaym", "Mombaim", "Mombaim", and "Bambaye" [4].

Disneyland Paris encompasses two theme parks, namely Disneyland Park and Walt Disney Studios Park [2][3]. These are the two parks at Euro Disney.

Ragtime music began to flourish in the United States during the 1890s [1][2]. It originated from African-American music styles such as jigs, cakewalks, and later became popular among various subcultures [3]. Ragtime is a synthesis of African syncopation and European classical music, specifically John Philip Sousa's marches [3]. The music became widely popular throughout North America during the start of the 20th century [3]. Ragtime was denounced as "degenerate" by conservatives and the classically trained establishment, but it continued to gain popularity and became mainstream [1][2].

Prior to 1973, mobile telephony was limited to phones installed in cars and other vehicles [4]. The prototype handheld phone used by Dr. Martin Cooper, a Motorola researcher and executive, was first made on April 3, 1973 [4]. The final scene of the film shows the family hiking on the Obersalzberg near the German town of Berchtesgaden, within sight of Adolf Hitler's Kehlsteinhaus Eagle's Nest retreat [4]. However, in reality, the family simply walked to the local train station and boarded a train to Italy [4].

This was a pivotal decision by creator Chris Chibnall as it focused the series more closely on Ellie Miller and improved the narrative structure [2]. The reveal of Joe Miller as the murderer attracted 8.8 million viewers at the start of the final episode, with a peak of 9.3 million viewers [3]. However, only 7.9 million viewers remained with the episode after the reveal [3]. The series averaged 9.2 million viewers per episode after accounting for time-delayed viewing [3].

In the Australian Singles Chart, "Wall to the Wall" peaked at number 21 [2]. The seven-day week, including Sunday as the day of rest, was established by Roman Emperor Constantine I in 321 AD [1]. The process of nitrogen gas release into the atmosphere is primarily associated with fossil fuel and biomass combustion, agricultural fertilizer application, and nitrification and denitrification processes in agroecosystems [1][2]. Nitrification is an aerobic process where microorganisms oxidize ammonium to nitrate, and denitrification is the anaerobic process where microorganisms reduce nitrate to atmospheric nitrogen gas [1][2]. Additionally, nitrogen oxides (NO) and nitrous oxide (N2O) are emitted as byproducts of these processes [1]. The nitrification process transforms ammonia into nitrate, while denitrification reduces nitrate to nitrogen gas through a series of steps involving nitrite, NO, and N2O [2]. Moreover, NO produced by industrial processes, automobiles, and agricultural fertilization, as well as NH emitted from soils, also contribute to the release of nitrogen gas into the atmosphere [1].

The Vikram Samvat calendar is named after King Vikramaditya of India [5]. It uses lunar months and solar sidereal years [1].

The Paschal candle is lit every year at Easter [1]. During the Easter service, the Paschal candle serves as the source of light for all other lights [2]. The candle remains lit at worship services throughout the Easter season and is located in the sanctuary close to the altar [2]. After the Easter season, it is frequently placed near the baptismal font [2]. Before 1955, the Paschal candle was also lit at services after Ascension, specifically during the Vigil of Pentecost [2]. During the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday, the ceremonial lighting of the Paschal candle is a significant moment [4]. During Maundy Thursday, all candles and lamps are extinguished, representing the darkness of a world without God, and the Paschal candle is lit [4]. The Paschal candle is used throughout the Paschal season and on special occasions such as baptisms and funerals [1].

There are five major circles of latitude, which are listed from north to south in a document [1]. These circles of latitude, excluding the Equator, mark the divisions between the five principal geographical zones [1]. The latitude of the other circles depends on the tilt of Earth's axis of rotation relative to its orbit [1]. The exact values of the other circles of latitude are not fixed [1].

The excretory system primarily expels substances through the kidneys, where products are excreted through urine [1]. The lungs also play a role in drug excretion, particularly through anesthetic gases [1].

The Inca Empire experienced a dramatic and quick decline following contact with the Spanish conquerors [2]. The single greatest cause of the decimation of native populations was infectious disease, as Old World Eurasian diseases, which had long been endemic on the Continent, were carried unknowingly by colonists and conquistadors [2]. Many aspects of Inca culture were systematically destroyed, including their sophisticated farming system [1]. Spanish colonial officials used the Inca mita corvée labor system for colonial aims, sometimes brutally [1]. The Inca Empire ultimately fell to the Spanish in 1533, when the last "Sapa Inca" of the empire, Atahualpa, was captured and executed [4].

The United States sees more tornadoes than any other country, with more than 1,200 tornadoes annually [1]. Most tornadoes in the United States occur east of the Rocky Mountains, with the Great Plains, Midwest, Mississippi Valley, and southern United States being particularly vulnerable [1]. However, tornadoes have been reported in every U.S state, including Alaska and Hawaii [2]. The state with the most tornadoes per unit area is Florida, though most are weak tornadoes of EF0 or EF1 intensity [3][4]. The state with the highest number of strong tornadoes per unit area is Oklahoma [3]. The Midwestern states are particularly prone to tornado activity, making up what is known as "Tornado Alley" [3].
